html:
A fellow acoustician asked me to answer this. I moved to industry only a little over a year ago, so my experience is limited, but here’s my take, based on my own path.

The biggest change is going from unlimited time to do one thing to limited time to do many things at once. Looking back, having so much time for a single project as a PhD student and postdoc was a real luxury. I’m not someone with a lot of intrinsic motivation, which is one of the reasons I fled academia. To get going I need a very concrete, real-world incentive. I don’t mean money; I mean that the work has practical value. Yet, to my surprise, even though I now have less time and more scattered work, I’m far more efficient than I was during my PhD, and that definitely has a lot to do with motivation and deadlines.

Second, R&D needs innovation, but innovation isn’t compulsory. R&D always starts from solving a practical problem, whereas research has to be novel. Take the two projects I’m working on right now. One uses machine learning for quality inspection. Whether you use an existing method or invent a new one, as long as it catches the defective products accurately, nobody cares how you did it. When it’s done, we update the software on the customer’s production line, and the workers there just press a button. Nobody there is going to ask: why did you use a GMM and not k-means? What they will care about is how long it takes to inspect one product, because if it’s too slow the boss is unhappy and output suffers. So algorithmic novelty doesn’t matter, but computation speed absolutely does. The other project optimizes an existing product. Just today I found a way to make one of its computational models faster and more accurate. Again, there’s no “innovation” and no chance of a paper, but the customer will be happy to use it, and the thought of a happy customer makes me even happier, so happy I almost want to volunteer for overtime. That kind of motivation and sense of achievement is something papers come nowhere near giving me.

Actually, you needn’t worry. A PhD plus a postdoc is enough to generalize your ability to learn: when you face a new problem, you’ll look at it from all sides, make a plan and find a solution.

As for expectations: I have indeed heard lots of PhD friends complain after moving to industry that the work is boring and unchallenging, and some have even gone back to academia. That varies from person to person. It depends on what kind of work and what kind of life you want.

One small insight after a year of working: the hardest part of the job isn’t the specific R&D or research problems, but how you conduct yourself. That covers a lot: how to get along with people, how to speak and act, how to manage your state of mind, how to plan your career. I recently went through a low patch of a month or two, and my confidence was shattered. I kept adjusting throughout, and now I’m finally starting to rebuild it, bit by bit. During this time I’ve come to see and understand some things that I think are more valuable than any knowledge I’ve learned. However focused you are on R&D, you are still a member of society, and you still have to deal with people. The art of getting along in the world is the most mysterious subject of all. Master its essence and it will serve you for life, whether you live in the East or the West.

Fanyu Meng · 108 consultations · rated 5.0 · Zhihu outstanding answerer in acoustics · PhD in acoustics, RWTH Aachen University
